PathSnap — Distributed Map-Matching & Route Reconstruction

Technical report · UE24CS352A Machine Learning Hackathon · PES University · Team PT_096
Team: Pradeep, Poojitha, Pandu, Pavan · Repository: https://github.com/GTX-Pradeep/Path_Snap_PT_096
Summary. Noisy GPS points are matched to the road network in two stages: a classifier scores the 8 nearest road segments of every GPS point, then an HMM/Viterbi decoder uses road connectivity to pick one connected route. Five classifier families were compared; LightGBM was selected and tuned with Bayesian optimisation. On the 10 student-test trips the final system reaches 92.43% pointwise accuracy (classifier only: 86.37%), route continuity 98.14% (classifier only: 93.54%) and route F1 0.920. The system runs as a FastAPI backend (Laptop 1) and a browser UI (Laptop 2).

1. Problem and approach

GPS fixes drift off the road (buildings, multipath, dropouts), so a vehicle appears on parallel streets or between roads. PathSnap reconstructs the road segments actually driven. Pipeline: clean GPS → project to metres → 8 candidate arcs per GPS point → 14 features per (point, candidate) → classifier probability that the candidate is the true arc → HMM/Viterbi over the candidates → one arc per GPS point and an ordered route. Laptop 1 hosts the model, decoder, road networks and evaluation; Laptop 2 hosts the UI.

2. Dataset understanding and exploratory data analysis

Partitions used: train (80 trips) for all fitting, cross-validation, Bayesian optimisation and decoder tuning; student_test (10 trips) for model comparison; evaluator_test (10 trips) only inside the API at demonstration time. All EDA below uses train + student_test (columns marked per partition).

2.1 How we preprocessed the data

  • Reading. .track (lon, lat, t), .nodes (lon, lat; row = node id), .arcs (from, to; row = arc id, directed), .route (ordered arc ids). Column order was verified per trip (longitude first, latitude second; all values in range). The trips are spread over several cities worldwide (latitudes −35° to 62°, longitudes −100° to 137°).
  • Cleaning. Drop NaN or out-of-range coordinates, sort by time, drop duplicate timestamps (none were found).
  • Projection. Degrees are angles and the metres-per-degree of longitude shrinks with latitude (at 56°N, 1° of longitude ≈ 0.56 of 1° of latitude), and the trips lie in different cities, so every trip is projected to a local equirectangular plane in metres centred on the trip.
  • Candidates. Arcs are sampled every 15 m into a KD-tree; the 8 nearest distinct arcs (exact point-to-segment distance) are the candidates of a GPS point.
  • Per-point labels. .route has no timestamps, so GPS points are aligned to it with a monotonic dynamic-programming alignment (route index never decreases, total point-to-arc distance minimised). A candidate is positive if it is the aligned arc (≈1 in 8 candidates).
  • Label cleaning (train only). Observations whose aligned reference arc is > 50 m away are removed from training (11% of training observations, mainly trips 33 and 54 whose reference route does not follow the GPS). Student-test is never filtered. Candidate miss rate (true arc not among the 8): train 8.2% → 0.85% after cleaning; student-test 0.35%.

2.3 Patterns observed and features extracted

GPS points lie near, not on, the roads (typically a few to ~20 m off); dense junctions and parallel roads create several plausible candidates; two-way roads are two directed arcs; some trips have long dropouts. The features answer these observations:

FeatureWhy
dist, dist_rank, dist_minus_min, dist_ratio_mincloseness to the GPS point, absolute and relative to the other candidates
heading_diff, heading_diff_cosGPS heading vs arc direction: separates the two directions of a road and crossing streets
proj_fracwhere on the segment the point projects (end points are ambiguous at junctions)
arc_lenshort connector arcs vs long road segments
speedlocal motion; heading is unreliable when the vehicle is slow
n_cand_30mlocal ambiguity (dense junctions)
dist_prev, dist_nexttemporal context: are the neighbouring GPS points also close to this arc?
out_degree, in_degreejunction structure around the arc

Interactive Folium map (EDA): maps/trip_train_00000010.html (raw GPS, reference route, road network, layer control); generated by src/make_map.py.

3. Model experimentation and comparison

Protocol (identical for every model). Candidate rows from the 80 training trips (label-cleaned) are used for 5-fold GroupKFold by trip (no trip in both training and validation folds) → CV macro F1; the model is refitted on all training rows and evaluated on the 10 student-test trips. Primary selection metric: observation-level Top-1 accuracy — for each GPS point the highest-scoring candidate is compared with the reference arc — because it is exactly the map-matching decision; log loss is used as a second criterion because the HMM consumes the probabilities. Seed 42 everywhere; logs in results/train_log.txt.

Route continuity here = share of consecutive GPS points whose argmax arcs are identical or directly connected (classifier only, before HMM).

Model selection. LightGBM had the best student-test Top-1 accuracy of the five untuned models, near-best log loss, the second-fastest training and sub-second inference, and a 1 MB model file — the best fit for a live API and for the sequential decoder. The MLP had the lowest log loss but needs a subsample to train in reasonable time; KNN overfits and is slow at inference; logistic regression underfits; random forest is close but larger and slower. LightGBM was therefore tuned (Section 4) and used as the final classifier.

3.2 Per-model questions

3.2.1 Logistic Regression (Linear / probabilistic)

A1. Why suitable? Each candidate is a yes/no decision (is this the true arc?), and logistic regression is the standard probabilistic baseline for that. It outputs calibrated probabilities that the HMM can use directly as emissions, trains in seconds, and its coefficients show how each feature pushes a candidate up or down.

A2. Strengths and limitations. Strengths: fast, interpretable, stable across folds, good probabilities. Limitations: a linear decision boundary cannot express interactions such as close AND same direction; balanced class weights give high recall but low precision.

B5. Important hyperparameters (initial values). StandardScaler; C=1.0, L2, class_weight=balanced, max_iter=1000. Trained on 1,383,341 candidate rows.

B6. Loss / objective. Binary cross-entropy (log loss) with L2 regularisation (C=1.0), lbfgs solver.

C7–C8. Student-test performance. Observation-level Top-1 accuracy 84.79%, candidate-level macro F1 0.829 (precision 0.583, recall 0.936), log loss 0.228; 5-fold group CV macro F1 0.826 ± 0.013; training time 7.5 s, inference on all 10 student-test trips 0.02 s. Route continuity of its argmax predictions is 92.15% (1503 breaks); with HMM decoding pointwise accuracy becomes 90.29%.

C9. Over- or underfitting? Slight underfitting, no overfitting. Train (0.826), CV (0.826) and student-test (0.829) macro F1 are almost equal but lower than the non-linear models: the model capacity, not the data, limits it.

3.2.2 Random Forest (Ensemble (bagging))

A1. Why suitable? The right arc depends on feature interactions (distance only matters if the heading also agrees). An ensemble of decision trees learns such rules without feature scaling and is robust to the outliers found in EDA (jumps, gaps). Averaging many trees on bootstrap samples gives stable probabilities.

A2. Strengths and limitations. Strengths: non-linear, robust, little tuning needed, feature importances. Limitations: slower to train and larger on disk (~8 MB) than linear or boosted models; probabilities are averaged votes, less sharp than boosting.

B5. Important hyperparameters (initial values). 100 trees, max_depth=12, min_samples_leaf=5, max_samples=0.2, balanced_subsample. Trained on 1,383,341 candidate rows.

B6. Loss / objective. Each tree minimises Gini impurity at every split; the forest averages tree probabilities.

C7–C8. Student-test performance. Observation-level Top-1 accuracy 85.49%, candidate-level macro F1 0.897 (precision 0.736, recall 0.942), log loss 0.140; 5-fold group CV macro F1 0.894 ± 0.020; training time 28.5 s, inference on all 10 student-test trips 0.20 s. Route continuity of its argmax predictions is 92.45% (1446 breaks); with HMM decoding pointwise accuracy becomes 92.28%.

C9. Over- or underfitting? Good fit. Train (0.897), CV (0.894 ± 0.020) and student-test (0.897) macro F1 are close, so it generalises to unseen trips without memorising the training trips.

3.2.3 K-Nearest Neighbours (Instance-based)

A1. Why suitable? A candidate that looks like training candidates that were correct is probably correct: KNN scores a candidate by the labels of its 25 most similar training candidates in standardised feature space. It is a non-parametric reference point with no training phase.

A2. Strengths and limitations. Strengths: no model assumptions, captures local structure. Limitations: memorises the training set, prediction cost grows with the number of stored rows (fitted on a 300k subsample, still the slowest inference), very sensitive to feature scaling, model file too large for GitHub (43 MB).

B5. Important hyperparameters (initial values). StandardScaler; k=25, distance-weighted; fitted on 300k-row subsample. Trained on 300,000 candidate rows.

B6. Loss / objective. No loss is optimised (lazy learner); prediction = distance-weighted vote of the 25 nearest neighbours (Euclidean distance on standardised features).

C7–C8. Student-test performance. Observation-level Top-1 accuracy 84.85%, candidate-level macro F1 0.907 (precision 0.852, recall 0.826), log loss 0.147; 5-fold group CV macro F1 0.901 ± 0.014; training time 0.6 s, inference on all 10 student-test trips 54.44 s. Route continuity of its argmax predictions is 91.94% (1544 breaks); with HMM decoding pointwise accuracy becomes 90.76%.

C9. Over- or underfitting? Overfitting. Train macro F1 (1.000) is clearly above CV (0.901) and student-test (0.907): the model fits its training rows much better than unseen trips.

3.2.4 LightGBM (Boosting)

A1. Why suitable? Gradient boosting adds trees one at a time, each correcting the errors of the previous ones, which suits tabular features with interactions. LightGBM's histogram algorithm trains on ~1.4M rows in seconds and predicts fast enough for the live API.

A2. Strengths and limitations. Strengths: strong accuracy on tabular data, fast training and inference, handles imbalance (is_unbalance), compact model (~1 MB). Limitations: many hyperparameters, can overfit with deep trees, less interpretable than a linear model.

B5. Important hyperparameters (initial values). 300 trees, lr=0.05, num_leaves=63, min_child_samples=50, subsample=0.8, colsample=0.8, is_unbalance. Trained on 1,383,341 candidate rows.

B6. Loss / objective. Binary log loss minimised by gradient boosting (second-order, leaf-wise trees).

C7–C8. Student-test performance. Observation-level Top-1 accuracy 86.04%, candidate-level macro F1 0.890 (precision 0.710, recall 0.955), log loss 0.142; 5-fold group CV macro F1 0.889 ± 0.018; training time 10.3 s, inference on all 10 student-test trips 0.54 s. Route continuity of its argmax predictions is 93.46% (1252 breaks); with HMM decoding pointwise accuracy becomes 92.41%.

C9. Over- or underfitting? Good fit. Train (0.900), CV (0.889 ± 0.018) and student-test (0.890) macro F1 are close, so it generalises to unseen trips without memorising the training trips.

3.2.5 MLP neural network (Neural network)

A1. Why suitable? A neural network can learn smooth non-linear combinations of all 14 features; it is the neural-network family required for comparison, and it is the only model here that produces an epoch-wise training history.

A2. Strengths and limitations. Strengths: flexible non-linear model, best-calibrated probabilities in our experiments (lowest log loss). Limitations: needs feature scaling and a subsample for training time, sensitive to learning rate and initialisation, a black box.

B5. Important hyperparameters (initial values). StandardScaler; hidden (64, 32) ReLU, Adam lr=1e-3, alpha=1e-4, batch 1024, early stopping; 500k-row subsample. Trained on 500,000 candidate rows.

B6. Loss / objective. Binary cross-entropy minimised with Adam (lr 1e-3), L2 penalty alpha=1e-4, early stopping on a 10% validation split.

C7–C8. Student-test performance. Observation-level Top-1 accuracy 85.65%, candidate-level macro F1 0.916 (precision 0.868, recall 0.841), log loss 0.099; 5-fold group CV macro F1 0.907 ± 0.017; training time 21.2 s, inference on all 10 student-test trips 0.05 s. Route continuity of its argmax predictions is 93.15% (1311 breaks); with HMM decoding pointwise accuracy becomes 92.37%.

C9. Over- or underfitting? Good fit. Train (0.914), CV (0.907 ± 0.017) and student-test (0.916) macro F1 are close, so it generalises to unseen trips without memorising the training trips.

The MLP stopped after 27 epochs (early stopping). The training loss fell from 0.1581 to 0.0951; validation accuracy is shown in the diagnostics figure (right panel). This is the only model with an epoch-wise history; no artificial curves are drawn for the others.

3.2.6 LightGBM (Bayesian-tuned) (Boosting (Bayesian-tuned))

A1. Why suitable? Gradient boosting adds trees one at a time, each correcting the errors of the previous ones, which suits tabular features with interactions. LightGBM's histogram algorithm trains on ~1.4M rows in seconds and predicts fast enough for the live API. This is the selected model, tuned with Bayesian optimisation (Section 4).

A2. Strengths and limitations. Strengths: strong accuracy on tabular data, fast training and inference, handles imbalance (is_unbalance), compact model (~1 MB). Limitations: many hyperparameters, can overfit with deep trees, less interpretable than a linear model.

B5. Important hyperparameters (initial values). n_estimators=450, learning_rate=0.01414, num_leaves=237, min_child_samples=32, subsample=0.7158, colsample_bytree=0.7388, reg_lambda=0.003947, reg_alpha=1.705, is_unbalance=False. Trained on 1,383,341 candidate rows.

B6. Loss / objective. Binary log loss minimised by gradient boosting (second-order, leaf-wise trees).

C7–C8. Student-test performance. Observation-level Top-1 accuracy 86.37%, candidate-level macro F1 0.918 (precision 0.869, recall 0.849), log loss 0.092; 5-fold group CV macro F1 0.913 ± 0.018; training time 18.3 s, inference on all 10 student-test trips 1.63 s. Route continuity of its argmax predictions is 93.54% (1237 breaks); with HMM decoding pointwise accuracy becomes 92.43%.

C9. Over- or underfitting? Good fit. Train (0.933), CV (0.913 ± 0.018) and student-test (0.918) macro F1 are close, so it generalises to unseen trips without memorising the training trips.

5. HMM and Viterbi route reconstruction

1. Hidden states. For GPS point i, the states are its 8 candidate arcs; state j at time i is always the arc cand[i, j], so the candidate-to-segment correspondence is preserved and the decoder returns one arc per GPS point.

2. Emissions. log P(candidate is the true arc) from the final classifier, multiplied by an emission weight w.

3. Transitions. Between consecutive points the vehicle drives along the network, so the network distance between the two matched positions should equal the straight GPS step: route_d = rest of arc a + shortest path(end of a → start of b) + part of arc b (Dijkstra on the directed road graph, arc lengths as weights, limit 1500 m); on the same arc, the signed progress (frac_b − frac_a)·length, so driving backwards is penalised. log T(a→b) = −|route_d − gps_d| / β.

Viterbi recurrence: δi+1(b) = maxa[δi(a) + log T(a,b)] + w·log ei+1(b), with back-pointers; the best final state is traced back.

4. Missing candidates and gaps. Points with fewer than 8 candidates are padded with impossible (−∞) states. If the time gap exceeds 30 s the transition is unconstrained (log T = 0), because after a dropout any road may be reached.

5. Disconnected segments. If arc b cannot be reached from arc a within the distance limit, log T = -30 (a large finite penalty rather than −∞): the decoder avoids such jumps but can still make one when the classifier is very confident, so a path always exists.

Decoder tuning. β and w were chosen by grid search on 20 training trips using out-of-fold classifier probabilities (each trip scored by a model that never saw it), objective = pointwise accuracy. Best: β = 1 m, w = 2 (accuracy 0.9351 vs classifier-only 0.8763 on those trips). Student-test and evaluator data were not used for tuning.

For the final model, pointwise accuracy rises from 86.37% to 92.43%, breaks fall from 1237 to 357 and route F1 from 0.858 to 0.920. The gain is largest for the weakest classifiers, because the transition model repairs isolated wrong choices.

Where HMM did not help. Trips 00000007 got worse with HMM. In trip 00000007 the vehicle is parked for the last ~175 points on a two-way road. At standstill the GPS heading is noise, the classifier prefers the opposite-direction twin arc, and the accumulated emission evidence outweighs one U-turn transition, so the decoder switches to the wrong direction although the route geometry is the same. A heading-reliability feature (speed-aware heading) is the planned fix; we report the case instead of hiding it.

6. Geographical visualisation using Folium

Interactive maps generated by our code (src/make_map.py, src/route_maps.py) are committed in maps/: raw GPS (blue), relevant road network (grey, toggle), reference route (green), classifier-only arcs (orange dashed) and the HMM-predicted route (red), with a legend, layer control and the extent fitted to the trip.

7. API, UI and deployment

Laptop 1 — API (api/main.py, FastAPI + uvicorn, port 8000). On start it loads models/lgbm_tuned.joblib and models/final_config.json. Endpoints: GET /health, GET /trips (the 10 evaluation trip ids), POST /predict {"trip_id": …}: loads the trip on the server, removes the reference route before prediction, runs candidates → features → classifier → HMM/Viterbi, then scores the prediction against the server-side reference route and returns GPS points, the predicted route geometry and the metrics. Every request is logged on the API console (trip, accuracy, continuity, route F1, time). Reference routes are never sent to the UI.

Laptop 2 — UI (ui/, static HTML/JS + Leaflet, served with python -m http.server 8080): enter the API address, see the 10 trips, click one → the UI posts the trip id to the API and shows the map (GPS, predicted route, classifier-only arcs) and the metrics.

Replace these two screenshots with ones taken on the two demonstration laptops (the guidelines ask for the CMD of the receiving laptop).

How to run: see the README (Laptop 1: run_api.bat; Laptop 2: run_ui.bat, then enter http://<laptop-1-IP>:8000).

Evaluator-test data were not used for training, model selection, hyperparameter or decoder tuning; predictions are not hardcoded.
